subsystems.name: Substrate
subsystems.role: the bulk material — waste plant matter that the fungus digests and binds together.
parts: straw, hemp hurd or corn stover

subsystems.name: Fungal inoculum
subsystems.role: the living binder: hyphae grow through the substrate and glue particles into a solid.
parts: white-rot fungal cultures (e.g. Pleurotus, Ganoderma, Trametes species)

subsystems.name: Moulds and growth chamber
subsystems.role: shape the brick and hold the warm, humid conditions the fungus needs.

subsystems.name: Setting and densification
subsystems.role: stops growth at the right moment and squeezes the material to raise its strength.

subsystems.name: Protection and finishing
subsystems.role: mycelium soaks up water and burns, so it needs treatment.

subsystems.name: Testing and quality control
subsystems.role: checks that a grown batch behaves like a building material.

buildSteps.title: Collect and prepare waste
buildSteps.detail: Agricultural residues are dried, chopped to a consistent size and pasteurised or sterilised so moulds and competing microbes are killed.

buildSteps.title: Inoculate
buildSteps.detail: Fungal spawn is mixed through the cooled substrate so hyphae have a food source and a head start.

buildSteps.title: Fill the moulds
buildSteps.detail: The inoculated mix is packed into brick-shaped moulds, sometimes around a timber or lattice core for extra stiffness.

buildSteps.title: Incubate
buildSteps.detail: Moulds sit in a warm, humid room for roughly one to two weeks while white hyphae spread through every gap, binding the particles.

buildSteps.title: Demould and stop growth
buildSteps.detail: Bricks are removed and dried or heat-treated, which kills the fungus so it cannot keep growing, fruit or rot later.

buildSteps.title: Press and finish
buildSteps.detail: Densifying under heat and pressure raises strength; coatings, fire retardants or laminated skins are then applied.

buildSteps.title: Cure, test and build
buildSteps.detail: Bricks are conditioned, tested for strength, density and fire behaviour, then laid with mortar or adhesives like conventional masonry.

prerequisites.tech: Fungal strain selection and sterile culture
prerequisites.why: different species give different density, strength and water resistance; contamination ruins a batch.
the process only makes sense if the feedstock is a waste stream, not a grown crop.
growing a few bricks in a lab is easy; growing thousands identically needs large, tightly controlled rooms.

prerequisites.tech: Waterproofing and fire treatment for bio-based material
prerequisites.why: untreated mycelium composite absorbs water and is combustible, which limits its use.
building codes and standards are written around fired clay, concrete and steel.

pathway.milestone: mycelium composites sold commercially as packaging, insulation and acoustic panels
pathway.unlocks: a proven growing and drying process and a real market for waste-fed materials.

pathway.milestone: non-load-bearing building products — internal partitions, tiles, decorative panels
pathway.unlocks: volume production experience and first building-code approvals.

pathway.milestone: hybrid structural elements, with mycelium as a core or infill inside timber or steel frames
pathway.unlocks: strength where conventional materials carry the load, plus insulation and carbon storage.

pathway.milestone: certified load-bearing blocks and grown-to-shape components that compost at end of life
pathway.unlocks: low-carbon walls that divert farm waste and return to soil — if water, fire and strength limits are solved.
